newsitem.title: LEBANON: Lebanon's Hariri lashes back during budget debate.
newsitem.headline: Lebanon's Hariri lashes back during budget debate.

text.p: Lebanon's Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri lashed out on Monday at MPs who criticised his government's repeated budget overruns and vowed that it would stick to its spending target in 1997.
He also angrily rejected a suggestion that parliament impose a ceiling on treasury bill issues which are the government's main tool for funding the public debt.
Hariri was stung during the five-day budget debate by several MPs who questioned the government's ability to stick to the 36 percent deficit of revenue against expenditure proposed in the budget.
The MPs pointed out that the government had failed to meet its targets for the past four years.

"If we were not keen to achieve the deficit noted we would not have presented (the budget) as such...We would have said the deficit would be 45 percent instead of 37 percent," Hariri replied before parliament began voting on the budget article-by-article.
The budget draft sets 1997 expenditure at 6,433 billion Lebanese pounds ($4.15 billion) against revenue of 4,100 billion -- a shortfall of 36 percent.
The 1996 deficit overran its 37.6 percent target to reach 51 percent. In 1994 and 1995, the deficit exceeded targets of 43 and 44 percent, reaching 57 and 47 percent.

The government has presented the 1997 budget as an attempt to restrain spending and slash the chronic deficits partly caused by heavy spending on Hariri's multi-billion dollar postwar reconstruction programme.

Hariri threatened to call for a vote of confidence when MPs, citing concern over the soaring public debt, demanded a cap on treasury bill issues. He said the budget allowed the government a free hand to raise funds to cover Treasury needs and the proposal could threaten the stability of the Lebanese currency.

"The issue of monetary stability is an essential corner of the government's policy," Hariri said. "If this article is touched then we cannot assume the responsibility for monetary stability in Lebanon and on this basis, we would demand a vote of confidence in the government."
Hariri's response angered speaker Nabih Berri who perceived it as an effort to limit parliament's oversight over legislation and threatened to call Hariri's bluff.
"We cannot be confronted with the issue of a vote of confidence every time we demand some amendment," Berri said. He threatened to set a confidence vote later.
Hariri admitted that government spending should be controlled but not at the expense of the reconstruction drive.
Responding to charges that his government was sinking Lebanon in debt while failing to implement productive economic policies, Hariri said: "Eighty percent of our debt is internal debt."
He said the deficit could be cut and debt repaid by boosting the productive sectors and increasing job opportunities.

Some MPs said the level of public indebtedness was disastrous. Total debt reached $10.348 billion at the end of December 1996, a figure which according to some MPs approaches Lebanon's estimated gross domestic product.
